title: Gather Victim Host Information
summary: Gathering victim host information is collection about individual systems rather than networks: administrative attributes such as host name and assigned address, and configuration specifics such as operating system, language, browser, and running software versions. Adversaries obtain it from active scanning and service banners, from phishing for information, from public data such as job postings and technical documents, and — distinctively — by compromising a website and adding content that fingerprints every visitor in the browser. User agent headers matter because they let a server-side operator decide, per visit, whether to deliver hostile content at all, which both narrows the target set and reduces the volume of payloads available for analysis. Telemetry therefore concentrates in web server access logs, where unusual user agent strings, requests to collection endpoints that appear on multiple unrelated sites, and uniform fingerprints across visitors become visible. The main analytic difficulty is that analytics platforms, content delivery networks, and consent tooling generate comparable traffic, so endpoint novelty and cross-site recurrence matter more than any single request.

beginner.definition: This technique is about learning about the individual computers inside a target network. It covers their names, their addresses, their operating systems, and the software they run. Attackers use these details to pick tools that will actually work on those machines.
beginner.whyItMatters: A computer's details decide which attack will work. Software written for one operating system often fails completely on another. If an attacker knows your systems, they avoid wasting effort on the wrong target. They can also build a payload that runs only where they want it to. That makes analysis harder for everyone else.
howItWorks: The attacker scans hosts and reads the banners that services send back when asked.
They record host names, addresses, and the services listening on each machine.
They collect operating system and software version details from the replies they receive.
They may add a small script to a website, which records visitor browser details.
They read user agent strings, which browsers send to describe themselves to servers.
With that list they choose tools and payloads that match the target machines.
beginner.example: Imagine a repair shop sending a technician to fix a printer in a large office. Before leaving, the technician asks one simple question at the desk. Is it a laser model from this year, or an older inkjet? That answer decides which tools and spare parts go into the van. Asking takes seconds and costs nothing. Arriving with the wrong parts wastes the entire visit. Gathering host information is that question, asked from a distance instead of at the desk. The attacker learns the make, model, and software level of each machine. Then the tools they bring are the ones most likely to work.
takeaways: Service banners and error pages should not announce exact software versions, because they help attackers choose tools.
Watch web servers for patterns that ask many hosts about many different services.
Keep an inventory of your hosts and software, so unexpected fingerprints stand out.

objectives: Explain what host information gathering collects and how it differs from network information gathering.
Describe how service banners and scanning reveal operating system and software versions.
Explain how user agent headers are used to select which visitors receive hostile content.
Identify web server log evidence of visitor fingerprinting from a compromised website.
Recommend configuration and inventory practices that limit host detail exposure.
